Socioeconomic Contributors of Chronic Disease in U.S. Counties¶

By: Dylan Sawransky and Martin Rosales

Project Website: https://dylan-sawransky.github.io/data-science-final-project/

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Dylan-Sawransky/data-science-final-project

Fall 2026 CMPS3160 - Milestone 2

1. Project Plan¶

Project Goal¶

Where you live predicts how long you live. In 2014, life expectancy differed by about 20 years between the U.S. counties with the lowest and highest values, and that gap had been widening since 1980 (Dwyer-Lindgren et al., 2017). Chronic conditions like diabetes and COPD are distributed just as unevenly across the country.

This project investigates which county-level socioeconomic conditions predict chronic disease prevalence across roughly 3,100 U.S. counties. The interesting question isn't whether poorer counties are less healthy; that is well established. The richest 1% of American men live about 14.6 years longer than the poorest 1% (Chetty et al., 2016), and a scientific review by the American Diabetes Association links lower income, food insecurity, lack of insurance and neighborhood conditions to higher diabetes risk (Hill-Briggs et al., 2021). What we want to know is whether any other factor predicts health outcomes independently of income.

If education, insurance coverage or healthcare access still matter after controlling for income, that points to targeted interventions. If they don't, that suggests that much of what looks like a healthcare access problem is really just a poverty problem.

Selected Datasets¶

  • Dataset 1 - 2025 CDC PLACES (Local Data for Better Health): our health outcomes

  • Dataset 2 - 2025 County Health Rankings & Roadmaps: our socioeconomic conditions


Question

Does any socioeconomic predictor retain significant explanatory power for chronic disease prevalence after controlling for median household income and rural/urban status?


How we will attack it

  1. Explanation: After controlling for income and rurality, are the share of adults with some college education, the share of adults without health insurance, primary care physician supply and unemployment still significantly associated with age-adjusted diabetes prevalence? (Model 1, hypothesis testing)
  2. Prediction: Does adding those conditions to an income-and-rurality model make diabetes prevalence more predictable in states the model has never seen? (Model 2, machine learning)

Diabetes is our primary outcome. COPD and obesity are secondary outcomes that show whether the pattern holds across conditions, and life expectancy serves as a check that does not rely on PLACES' modeling (see below).

How Data Addresses Our Question¶

Both datasets are published at county level and keyed on the five-digit FIPS county code, which makes them directly joinable. PLACES supplies our dependent variables (disease prevalence) while County Health Rankings supplies the independent variables (socioeconomic conditions). After merging on FIPS, each row represents one county with both its health outcomes and its community conditions attached.

Why this data is the right fit. PLACES is the only source that gives comparable chronic disease estimates for nearly every U.S. county, and County Health Rankings gathers income, education, insurance, physician supply, unemployment and rurality for the same counties in one file. Together they cover every variable in our question at the same geographic level. Two features of the data shape how we read the results:

  • PLACES values are model-based estimates. CDC predicts each county's prevalence from survey responses using respondents' age, sex, race/ethnicity and education, plus the county poverty rate (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2025a). CDC advises caution when these estimates are used in regressions with similar variables (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2025c), because part of any education or poverty association can be built into the estimates. To guard against this, we also check our findings against life expectancy, which County Health Rankings computes from death records rather than from a survey model.
  • Kentucky and Pennsylvania are absent from PLACES 2025. Section 2 explains why and how we handle it.

Analysis Approach: Controlling for Income¶

Several of our candidate predictors are themselves linked to income, so how we "control for income" determines whether our answer means anything.

  • Income enters every model as a control, on a log scale. The relationship between income and diabetes is curved (EDA 6): an extra $10,000 matters far more in a $40,000 county than in a $120,000 one. Log income captures that diminishing return; a straight line in dollars would leave income effects behind for other variables to absorb. Percent rural is the second control.
  • "Controlling for" means comparing counties with the same income and rurality. In a multiple regression, each predictor's coefficient describes how diabetes differs between counties that have the same income and rurality but differ on that predictor. In the EDA we preview this with partial correlations: remove what the controls explain from both the predictor and diabetes, then correlate what is left.
  • Child poverty belongs with income, not with the "other factors". It is another way of measuring household income (correlation −0.83 with log income, EDA 5), so we report it but do not treat a child poverty association as evidence that something other than income matters.
  • Insurance is partly a consequence of income. Lower-wage jobs are less likely to come with health benefits, so uninsurance and income move together. A significant uninsurance coefficient would mean that insurance coverage carries information beyond what income tells us, not that being uninsured causes diabetes. There is also a measurement twist: PLACES counts diagnosed diabetes, and uninsured adults are less likely to be diagnosed, which could weaken or even reverse the observed association.
  • We check that the variables can be told apart. Variance inflation factors confirm the predictors are not so tangled with income that a regression cannot separate them (EDA 5).

Raw Dataset 1¶

Source: CDC PLACES County Data

Documentation: About PLACES · PLACES methodology

Data Description:

PLACES provides model-based small-area estimates of 40 health measures for every U.S. county, covering chronic disease outcomes, preventive service use, health risk behaviors, disability, health status and health-related social needs. It is a collaboration between the CDC, the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation and the CDC Foundation (Greenlund et al., 2022).

Data Collection:

All 40 county measures come from one source: the Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System (BRFSS), a state-based random digit dial telephone survey of U.S. adults. Most counties have too few respondents for a direct estimate, so CDC fits a multilevel regression model to the survey and applies it to each county's Census population (multilevel regression and poststratification) (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2025a). The 2025 release uses 2023 BRFSS data for most measures.

How it answers our question: PLACES provides the dependent variables: age-adjusted prevalence of diabetes, COPD and obesity for each county.

Raw Dataset 2¶

Source: CHR&R Data & Documentation

Data Description:

Published annually by the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation and the University of Wisconsin Population Health Institute, this dataset covers 3,000+ counties with measures spanning median household income, unemployment, educational attainment, uninsured rate, food insecurity, air quality, housing problems and primary care physician ratios (County Health Rankings & Roadmaps, 2025).

Data Collection:

CHR is a compilation rather than a survey. It assembles measures from many federal sources such as the NCHS vital statistics, Census/ACS, BLS, FBI UCR, EPA and HUD. Each measure keeps its source's reference period, so a 2025 release does not mean every value was collected in 2025.

How it answers our question: CHR provides the independent variables (income, rurality, education, insurance, physician supply, unemployment) and life expectancy for our robustness check.

The raw file has an unusual layout: the first data row repeats the column names as short codes, and the next rows are the national and state totals. We remove both during cleaning.

Cleaned Dataset 1¶

Step 1: Select the measures we need. Of the 167 columns, we keep the identifiers, population and three outcomes. Each PLACES measure comes in a crude and an age-adjusted version, and we use the age-adjusted version for every outcome in this notebook. Chronic diseases become more common with age and rural counties tend to be older, so crude prevalence would partly measure a county's age structure. Age adjustment re-weights every county to the same standard age distribution, which is what CDC recommends for comparing counties (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2025c). The printout shows the difference is not trivial: crude diabetes prevalence runs up to 9 points above the age-adjusted figure.

In [29]:
# Age-adjusted prevalence for our primary outcome and two secondary outcomes
PLACES_MEASURES = {
    "diabetes_adjprev": "diabetes_pct",   # primary outcome: diagnosed diabetes
    "copd_adjprev":     "copd_pct",       # secondary outcome
    "obesity_adjprev":  "obesity_pct",    # secondary outcome
}
OUTCOMES = list(PLACES_MEASURES.values())

places_clean = (places[["countyfips", "stateabbr", "countyname", "totalpopulation",
                        *PLACES_MEASURES]]
                .rename(columns={"countyfips": "fips", "stateabbr": "state",
                                 "countyname": "county", "totalpopulation": "population",
                                 **PLACES_MEASURES}))

# How far apart are the crude and age-adjusted diabetes estimates?
gap = places["diabetes_crudeprev"] - places["diabetes_adjprev"]
print(f"Crude minus age-adjusted diabetes: median {gap.median():.1f} points, "
      f"range {gap.min():.1f} to {gap.max():.1f} points")
places_clean.head()

Step 2: Standardize county identifiers. pandas reads countyfips as an integer, which drops leading zeros (Alabama's Autauga County, 01001, becomes 1001). We pad it back to a 5-character string and check that every code is five digits and unique, which is essential for an error-free merge with Dataset 2.

In [30]:
print("Before:", places_clean["fips"].dtype, places_clean["fips"].head(3).tolist())

# Rebuild the 5-digit FIPS string (2-digit state + 3-digit county)
places_clean["fips"] = places_clean["fips"].astype(str).str.zfill(5)
assert places_clean["fips"].str.fullmatch(r"\d{5}").all(), "Malformed FIPS code"
assert places_clean["fips"].is_unique, "Duplicate county identifiers"

print("After: ", places_clean["fips"].dtype, places_clean["fips"].head(3).tolist())

After:  object ['21221', '21231', '21229']

The missing counties are every county in Kentucky (120) and Pennsylvania (67). Neither state collected enough BRFSS data in 2023 to meet the survey's minimum requirements, so CDC could not produce estimates for them in this release (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2025b). Filling them in would mean layering our own guess on top of a model-based estimate, so we drop them. Our results therefore describe the other 48 states and DC; because eastern Kentucky is part of Appalachia, a region with high diabetes rates, this is a limitation we carry forward.

Step 4: Drop the missing counties and set data types. FIPS and county names are text identifiers, state is a category, population is an integer and the outcomes are decimal percentages.

In [32]:
places_clean = places_clean.dropna(subset=OUTCOMES).reset_index(drop=True)

# Explicitly set data types: identifiers are text, the state is a category
places_clean = places_clean.astype({"fips": "string", "state": "category",
                                    "county": "string", "population": "int64"})

print("Cleaned Dataset 1 information:")
places_clean.info()
print(f"\nRemaining records: {len(places_clean):,} (original: {len(places):,})")

Summary of Dataset 1 (PLACES) Cleaning & Structure¶

What was done during cleaning:¶

  1. Feature Selection: Filtered down from 167 variables to the 3 age-adjusted outcome measures we study (diabetes, copd, obesity) alongside identifiers (fips, state, county) and population.
  2. Standardized County Identifiers: Padded the FIPS code with leading zeros to a uniform 5-digit string (e.g., '02020') and confirmed every code is unique.
  3. Handling Missing Values: Traced the 187 counties without estimates to Kentucky and Pennsylvania, explained why they are missing, and removed them (3,143 → 2,956 counties).
  4. Explicit Datatype Alignment: Identifiers as strings, state as a category, population as an integer and prevalence measures as float64.


What the cleaned dataset shows:¶

A tidy 7-column table for 2,956 U.S. counties in 48 states and DC. For each county it gives the estimated age-adjusted percentage of adults with diagnosed diabetes, COPD and obesity.

Cleaned Dataset 2¶

Step 1: Remove rows that are not counties. We drop the row of variable codes, then the national row and the state summary rows, which all have county code 000. Keeping them would count each state twice (once as itself and once as the sum of its counties).

In [33]:
# Row 0 repeats the header as short variable codes (e.g. "v063_rawvalue"), so drop it
chr_clean = chr_raw.iloc[1:].copy()
chr_clean["fips"] = chr_clean["5-digit FIPS Code"].astype(str).str.zfill(5)

# County code "000" marks the national row and each state's summary row
is_summary = chr_clean["County FIPS Code"].astype(str).str.zfill(3) == "000"
print(f"National/state summary rows removed: {is_summary.sum()}")
chr_clean = chr_clean.loc[~is_summary]
print(f"County rows remaining: {len(chr_clean):,}")

National/state summary rows removed: 52
County rows remaining: 3,152

Step 2: Select and rename the variables in our question. CHR has 796 columns. We keep the controls, the four predictors, child poverty (to examine its overlap with income) and life expectancy (our non-modeled check), and give them short names:

Our name CHR measure Role
median_household_income Median household income ($) Control
rural_pct % of population living in rural areas Control
some_college_pct % of adults ages 25–44 with some post-secondary education Predictor
uninsured_adults_pct % of adults under 65 without health insurance Predictor
pcp_per_100k Primary care physicians per 100,000 residents Predictor
unemployment_pct % of the labor force unemployed Predictor
child_poverty_pct % of children living in poverty Income measure
life_expectancy Life expectancy at birth (years), from death records Robustness outcome

Because of the code row, pandas reads every column as text, so we convert them to numbers here.

In [34]:
CHR_VARS = {
    "Median Household Income raw value": "median_household_income",
    "% Rural raw value":                 "rural_pct",
    "Some College raw value":            "some_college_pct",
    "Uninsured Adults raw value":        "uninsured_adults_pct",
    "Primary Care Physicians raw value": "pcp_per_100k",
    "Unemployment raw value":            "unemployment_pct",
    "Children in Poverty raw value":     "child_poverty_pct",
    "Life Expectancy raw value":         "life_expectancy",
}
socio = chr_clean[["fips", *CHR_VARS]].rename(columns=CHR_VARS)
numeric_cols = list(CHR_VARS.values())

# The code row made pandas read every column as text; convert to numbers.
# errors="coerce" turns blank cells into NaN instead of raising an error.
socio[numeric_cols] = socio[numeric_cols].apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce")
socio.head(3)

Step 3: Put every variable in readable units. CHR stores percentages as proportions (0.61 rather than 61%), so we multiply them by 100 to match PLACES. Physician supply is stored per resident, so we rescale it to the standard rate per 100,000.

In [35]:
# CHR stores percentages as proportions (0.42 = 42%); rescale to match PLACES
pct_cols = [c for c in numeric_cols if c.endswith("_pct")]
socio[pct_cols] = socio[pct_cols] * 100

# Physician supply is stored per resident; convert to the usual rate per 100,000
socio["pcp_per_100k"] = socio["pcp_per_100k"] * 100_000

socio["fips"] = socio["fips"].astype("string")
assert socio["fips"].is_unique
socio.describe().T

Summary of Dataset 2 (CHR) Cleaning & Structure¶

What was done during cleaning:¶

  1. Removed Non-County Rows: Dropped the variable-code row and 52 national and state summary rows.
  2. Feature Selection: Kept 8 of 796 measures, renamed to short descriptive names.
  3. Unit Conversion: Converted proportions to percentages and physician supply to a rate per 100,000.
  4. Explicit Datatype Alignment: Converted all measures from text to float64, with blank cells coerced to NaN.


What the cleaned dataset shows:¶

One row per county (3,152 rows) describing each county's economic conditions, education, insurance coverage, access to primary care, rurality and life expectancy.

Merged Dataset¶

Step 1: Join the datasets on FIPS and audit the result. We use an outer join with an indicator column so that any county that fails to match is visible rather than silently lost. validate="one_to_one" makes pandas raise an error if either table contains a duplicate county.

In [37]:
# Outer join + indicator shows every county that fails to match;
# validate="one_to_one" raises an error if either table has duplicate counties
merged = places_clean.merge(socio, on="fips", how="outer",
                            validate="one_to_one", indicator=True)
print(merged["_merge"].value_counts().to_string())

STATE_FIPS = {"21": "Kentucky", "42": "Pennsylvania", "09": "Connecticut", "48": "Texas"}
chr_only = merged.loc[merged["_merge"] == "right_only", "fips"].str[:2]
print("\nCounties found only in CHR, by state:")
print(chr_only.value_counts().rename(index=lambda s: STATE_FIPS.get(s, s)).to_string())

Every PLACES county found its match. The 196 counties that appear only in CHR are:

  • 187 Kentucky and Pennsylvania counties, which have no PLACES estimates (Step 3 above).
  • 8 Connecticut rows for the state's old counties. The Census Bureau replaced Connecticut's 8 counties with 9 planning regions in 2022 (Census county changes). Both datasets report the planning regions, which matched; CHR also keeps empty rows for the old counties.
  • 1 Texas county, Loving County, with 43 residents, which is too small for PLACES to estimate.

Step 2: Build the final table. We keep the 2,956 matched counties and add four derived columns: log income and log physician supply (both are heavily right-skewed, EDA 2), plus income quartiles and rurality groups for comparisons. The table is saved as a CSV, which we also upload to the repository.

In [38]:
county = merged.loc[merged["_merge"] == "both"].drop(columns="_merge").copy()
county["population"] = county["population"].astype("int64")   # outer join made it float

# Derived variables used in the EDA and models
county["log_income"] = np.log(county["median_household_income"])
county["log_pcp"] = np.log1p(county["pcp_per_100k"])           # log1p handles 0 physicians
county["income_group"] = pd.qcut(county["median_household_income"], 4,
    labels=["Lowest income", "Lower middle", "Upper middle", "Highest income"])
county["rurality"] = pd.cut(county["rural_pct"], bins=[-0.01, 20, 50, 80, 100],
    labels=["Urban (<20%)", "Mixed (20-50%)", "Mostly rural (50-80%)", "Rural (>80%)"])

county = county.sort_values("fips").reset_index(drop=True)
county.to_csv("county_health_cleaned.csv", index=False)

print(f"Final table: {county.shape[0]:,} counties x {county.shape[1]} columns\n")
print(county.dtypes.to_string())
county.head()

Summary of Merged Dataset¶

What was done during merging:¶

  1. Validated Join: Joined on FIPS with a one-to-one check and audited all 196 unmatched rows.
  2. Derived Variables: Added log_income, log_pcp, income_group (quartiles) and rurality (four groups).


What the merged dataset shows:¶

A tidy table of 2,956 counties × 19 columns: each row is one county, each column is one variable, and each cell holds one value (Wickham, 2014). This table is the starting point for all of the analysis below.

3. Exploratory Data Analysis¶

Each result below is produced by an executable cell. The unit of analysis is a county, not an individual person, and counties are weighted equally, so the results describe how conditions vary between counties. (A county of 500 people counts as much as Los Angeles County.)

EDA 1: Define the analysis sample¶

Every analysis below uses the same set of counties, so that differences between results reflect the data rather than a changing sample. We keep counties that have all three outcomes, both controls and all predictors, and report what is dropped.

In [39]:
CONTROLS = ["log_income", "rural_pct"]
PREDICTORS = ["some_college_pct", "uninsured_adults_pct", "log_pcp", "unemployment_pct"]
LABELS = {
    "diabetes_pct": "Diabetes (%)", "copd_pct": "COPD (%)", "obesity_pct": "Obesity (%)",
    "life_expectancy": "Life expectancy (yrs)", "median_household_income": "Median income ($)",
    "log_income": "log(median income)", "rural_pct": "Rural (%)",
    "some_college_pct": "Some college (%)", "uninsured_adults_pct": "Uninsured adults (%)",
    "pcp_per_100k": "PCPs per 100k", "log_pcp": "log(1 + PCPs per 100k)",
    "unemployment_pct": "Unemployment (%)", "child_poverty_pct": "Child poverty (%)",
}

analysis = county.dropna(subset=OUTCOMES + CONTROLS + PREDICTORS + ["child_poverty_pct"]).copy()
print(f"Complete-case sample: {len(analysis):,} / {len(county):,} counties")
print("Counties dropped for each missing variable:")
print(county[CONTROLS + PREDICTORS].isna().sum().loc[lambda s: s > 0].to_string())

Complete-case sample: 2,799 / 2,956 counties
Counties dropped for each missing variable:
log_income                1
uninsured_adults_pct      1
log_pcp                 156
unemployment_pct         10

What it shows: 2,799 of the 2,956 merged counties (95%) have complete data. Almost all of the 157 exclusions are small counties with no reported primary care physician rate. These are mostly very small, rural counties, so the sample slightly under-represents the most remote places.

Calculate the mean, median, spread, range and skew of every variable. The scale and skew tell us whether variables need transforming before modeling. The highest-prevalence counties are ranked by modeled point estimates, not by proven disease burden.

What it shows:

  • The typical county has an age-adjusted diabetes prevalence of 10.7% (median), but values range from 6.0% to 23.8%, a nearly fourfold difference. The distribution is right-skewed (skew 1.06), so the mean (11.1%) sits above the median.
  • Median income (skew 1.39) and physician supply (skew 2.14) have long right tails: a few wealthy suburbs and medical hubs sit far above everyone else. We therefore use the log of both in our models.
  • The ten highest-prevalence counties are in South Dakota's Lakota reservations (Oglala Lakota, Todd), the Texas border region, the Alabama Black Belt and the Mississippi Delta. **All ten have median incomes below $51,000**, under the national county median of about $63,000.

EDA 3: Income quartiles¶

Divide counties into four equally sized income groups and compare diabetes prevalence. This shows how large the income gradient is that our controls need to absorb. It is descriptive and not a causal effect.

In [41]:

What it shows: Mean prevalence falls steadily from 13.6% in the lowest-income quartile to 9.4% in the highest, a gap of 4.2 percentage points. The drop is steepest between the bottom two groups (2.3 points) and smaller after that, a first sign that the income relationship is curved. The lowest-income quartile is also the most spread out (standard deviation 2.35 vs. about 1.3 elsewhere), so among poor counties there is room for factors other than income to matter.

EDA 4: Income and rurality (cross-tabulation)¶

Rurality is our second control. Rural counties tend to be poorer, so we cross-tabulate the two to check whether rurality adds anything within the same income level or simply stands in for income.

What it shows: The cross-tab confirms that income and rurality are intertwined: 375 of the 682 lowest-income counties are more than 80% rural, while the largest group among the highest-income counties is urban. The heatmap separates the two:

  • Reading down any column, diabetes falls by roughly 4 to 5 points from the lowest to the highest income quartile.
  • Reading across any row, rurality makes little difference. Within the lowest-income quartile, urban counties have the highest mean (14.8%, though only 29 counties).

So rural counties' higher average diabetes is largely an income effect. Rurality stays in the model as a control so that the predictors are compared between counties that are similar on both.

EDA 5: Correlation matrix¶

Pearson correlation describes linear relationships. Beyond each variable's correlation with diabetes, the matrix shows how much the predictors overlap with income and with each other. If two variables move almost in lockstep, a regression cannot separate their effects. Variance inflation factors (VIFs) quantify this. A correlation alone cannot identify causation or isolate each factor's independent contribution.

In [43]:
corr_cols = ["diabetes_pct", "log_income", "child_poverty_pct", "rural_pct"] + PREDICTORS
corr_matrix = analysis[corr_cols].corr()
print("Correlation of each variable with diabetes:")
print(corr_matrix["diabetes_pct"].drop("diabetes_pct").rename(LABELS).round(3).to_string())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6.5))
mask = np.triu(np.ones_like(corr_matrix, dtype=bool), k=1)   # show each pair once
sns.heatmap(corr_matrix.rename(index=LABELS, columns=LABELS), mask=mask, annot=True, fmt=".2f",
            cmap=DIVERGING, vmin=-1, vmax=1, linewidths=2, linecolor="white",
            cbar_kws={"label": "Pearson correlation"}, ax=ax)
ax.set(title="County-level correlations")
ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=35)
plt.setp(ax.get_xticklabels(), ha="right")
ax.grid(False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Variance inflation factors: can a regression separate these variables?
def vif_table(columns):
    X = sm.add_constant(analysis[columns])
    return pd.Series([variance_inflation_factor(X.values, i) for i in range(1, X.shape[1])],
                     index=[LABELS[c] for c in columns])
vifs = pd.DataFrame({"planned model": vif_table(CONTROLS + PREDICTORS),
                     "+ child poverty": vif_table(CONTROLS + ["child_poverty_pct"] + PREDICTORS)})
print("\nVariance inflation factors (rule of thumb: concern above 5):")
print(vifs.round(2).to_string(na_rep="-"))

Uninsured adults (%)      0.49

Variance inflation factors (rule of thumb: concern above 5):
                        planned model  + child poverty
Child poverty (%)                   -             4.05
Rural (%)                        1.47             1.52
Some college (%)                 1.99             2.05
Unemployment (%)                 1.21             1.32
Uninsured adults (%)             1.34             1.39
log(1 + PCPs per 100k)           1.24             1.25
log(median income)               1.81             3.73

What it shows:

  • Child poverty is the variable most strongly correlated with diabetes (0.82), but it is essentially income measured another way (−0.83 with log income). Adding it to the model roughly doubles the VIF of log income (1.81 → 3.73). This is why we treat it as part of income rather than as a separate factor.
  • Education overlaps most with income among the predictors (0.61), followed by uninsurance (−0.38). Unemployment and physician supply overlap less.
  • Every VIF in the planned model is below 2, far under the usual concern threshold of 5. The predictors share information with income, but each has enough independent variation for a regression to estimate it separately.

EDA 6: Income versus diabetes¶

Each point represents one county. We fit a straight line on the raw dollar scale and on the log scale to decide how income should enter our models.

In [44]:
def linear_r2(x, y):
    """R-squared of a simple straight-line fit of y on x."""
    return sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(x)).fit().rsquared

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.3), sharey=True)
y = analysis["diabetes_pct"]
for ax, x, xlabel, title in [
        (axes[0], analysis["median_household_income"] / 1000,
         "Median household income ($ thousands)", "Raw income scale"),
        (axes[1], analysis["log_income"], "log(median household income)", "Log income scale")]:
    ax.scatter(x, y, s=8, alpha=0.25, color=BLUE, edgecolors="none")
    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
    grid = np.linspace(x.min(), x.max(), 100)
    ax.plot(grid, intercept + slope * grid, color=ORANGE, linewidth=2,
            label=f"Linear fit, R² = {linear_r2(x, y):.3f}")
    ax.set(xlabel=xlabel, title=title)
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right")
axes[0].set(ylabel="Diabetes prevalence (%, age-adjusted)")
fig.suptitle("County income and estimated diabetes prevalence", fontweight="bold")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

What it shows: On the raw dollar scale (left) the cloud of points curves: diabetes drops quickly between $30,000 and $60,000 and then levels off. A straight line misses this, overshooting at both ends and predicting under 2% for the wealthiest county, lower than any county actually has. On the log scale (right) the relationship is much closer to a straight line, and the share of variation explained rises from R² = 0.40 to 0.48. This is the reason every model in this project controls for log income.

EDA 7: Education versus diabetes¶

The left panel checks whether counties with more adults having some college education have different diabetes prevalence. The right panel repeats the comparison after removing what log income and percent rural explain from both variables. It shows each county relative to counties with similar income and rurality.

In [45]:
def residualize(values, controls):
    """What is left of `values` after an OLS regression on `controls` (plus intercept)."""
    return sm.OLS(values, sm.add_constant(controls)).fit().resid

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.3))
panels = [
    (axes[0], analysis["some_college_pct"], analysis["diabetes_pct"],
     "Some college (%)", "Diabetes prevalence (%)", "Before adjustment"),
    (axes[1], residualize(analysis["some_college_pct"], analysis[CONTROLS]),
     residualize(analysis["diabetes_pct"], analysis[CONTROLS]),
     "Some college, relative to similar counties (pts)",
     "Diabetes, relative to similar counties (pts)",
     "After adjusting for log income and % rural"),
]
for ax, x, y, xlabel, ylabel, title in panels:
    ax.scatter(x, y, s=8, alpha=0.25, color=BLUE, edgecolors="none")
    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
    grid = np.linspace(x.min(), x.max(), 100)
    ax.plot(grid, intercept + slope * grid, color=ORANGE, linewidth=2,
            label=f"r = {np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1]:.2f}")
    ax.set(xlabel=xlabel, ylabel=ylabel, title=title)
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right")
fig.suptitle("County education and estimated diabetes prevalence", fontweight="bold")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

What it shows: Before adjustment, education and diabetes are strongly related (r = −0.65). After adjustment the relationship weakens to r = −0.45 but remains clearly visible. Roughly a third of the raw association is shared with income and rurality, and the rest is not. A county with more college-educated adults than similar-income counties tends to have less diabetes than those counties. This is the core pattern our research question is about.

EDA 8: Controlling for income and rurality (partial correlations)¶

A partial correlation removes the best-fitting relationship with log income and percent rural from both diabetes and each predictor, then correlates what remains. This answers whether an association remains after adjustment, but it does not remove every possible confounder.

In [46]:
def partial_corr(df, outcome, predictor, controls):
    """Correlation of outcome and predictor after both are adjusted for the controls."""
    return np.corrcoef(residualize(df[outcome], df[controls]),
                       residualize(df[predictor], df[controls]))[0, 1]

candidates = PREDICTORS + ["child_poverty_pct"]
partials = pd.DataFrame({
    "raw r": [analysis[["diabetes_pct", p]].corr().iloc[0, 1] for p in candidates],
    "partial r (log income + % rural)": [partial_corr(analysis, "diabetes_pct", p, CONTROLS)
                                         for p in candidates],
}, index=[LABELS[p] for p in candidates])
display(partials)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.4))
order = partials.index[::-1]
ypos = np.arange(len(order))
ax.barh(ypos + 0.2, partials.loc[order, "raw r"], height=0.38, color=GRAY, label="Raw correlation")
ax.barh(ypos - 0.2, partials.loc[order, "partial r (log income + % rural)"], height=0.38,
        color=BLUE, label="After adjusting for log income and % rural")
ax.set_yticks(ypos, order)
ax.axvline(0, color="#0b0b0b", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set(title="Correlation with diabetes, before and after income adjustment",
       xlabel="Correlation with diabetes prevalence")
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.22), ncol=2, fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
raw r partial r (log income + % rural)
Some college (%) -0.65 -0.45
Uninsured adults (%) 0.50 0.36
log(1 + PCPs per 100k) -0.17 -0.14
Unemployment (%) 0.36 0.18
Child poverty (%) 0.82 0.60

What it shows:

  • Education (−0.45) and uninsurance (+0.36) keep substantial associations after adjustment. These are the two strongest candidates for factors that matter independently of income.
  • Unemployment (0.18) and physician supply (−0.14) shrink to weak associations once income is accounted for.
  • Child poverty stays high (0.60), but this does not mean "something besides income" matters. Child poverty captures the bottom of a county's income distribution, which the median misses. PLACES also uses county poverty when generating its estimates (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2025a), so part of this correlation is built in.

EDA 9: Multiple regression with income adjustment¶

Fit diabetes prevalence on the two controls and all four predictors together. Variables are standardized, so each coefficient is the change in diabetes prevalence (percentage points) for a one-standard-deviation increase holding everything else in the model constant. Standard errors are heteroskedasticity-robust (HC3). This is a preliminary, observational fit that does not establish causation.

In [47]:
# Standardize predictors so coefficients are comparable (effect of a 1-SD change)
X_cols = CONTROLS + PREDICTORS
X = sm.add_constant((analysis[X_cols] - analysis[X_cols].mean()) / analysis[X_cols].std())
y = analysis["diabetes_pct"]

baseline = sm.OLS(y, X[["const"] + CONTROLS]).fit(cov_type="HC3")
full = sm.OLS(y, X).fit(cov_type="HC3")

results = pd.DataFrame({"coef (pts per 1 SD)": full.params, "robust SE": full.bse,
                        "p-value": full.pvalues,
                        "95% CI low": full.conf_int()[0], "95% CI high": full.conf_int()[1]})
display(results.drop("const").rename(index=LABELS).style.format(
    {"p-value": "{:.2g}"}, precision=3))

print(f"R² with controls only:         {baseline.rsquared:.3f}")
print(f"R² with controls + predictors: {full.rsquared:.3f}")

# Do the leftover errors cluster by state?
state_fit = sm.OLS(full.resid, pd.get_dummies(analysis["state"].astype(str), dtype=float)).fit()
print(f"Share of the remaining variation explained by state alone: {state_fit.rsquared:.1%}")
  coef (pts per 1 SD) robust SE p-value 95% CI low 95% CI high
log(median income) -1.149 0.045 7.7e-142 -1.238 -1.060
Rural (%) -0.584 0.032 7.3e-76 -0.646 -0.522
Some college (%) -0.690 0.041 2.7e-64 -0.770 -0.610
Uninsured adults (%) 0.416 0.031 8.5e-42 0.356 0.476
log(1 + PCPs per 100k) -0.142 0.033 1.5e-05 -0.206 -0.078
Unemployment (%) 0.171 0.032 9.5e-08 0.108 0.234 
R² with controls only:         0.512
R² with controls + predictors: 0.644
Share of the remaining variation explained by state alone: 40.3%

What it shows:

  • Income and rurality alone explain 51.2% of the variation in diabetes across counties. Adding the four predictors raises this to 64.4%, so these conditions carry real information beyond income.
  • Education has the largest effect among the predictors: one standard deviation more adults with some college (about 12 percentage points) goes with 0.69 points less diabetes. One standard deviation more uninsured adults (about 6 points) goes with 0.42 points more.
  • Physician supply (−0.14) and unemployment (+0.17) are much smaller.
  • With income and the other predictors held fixed, rural counties have slightly lower diabetes (−0.58 per SD), consistent with EDA 4.
  • Caution about the p-values: all predictors look highly significant here, but 40% of the leftover variation lines up with state boundaries. Counties in the same state share policies and conditions, so they are not independent observations. Our final model clusters standard errors by state, which will give wider and more honest confidence intervals, and the two weakest predictors may not survive.

EDA 10: Compare disease outcomes¶

Check whether the adjusted associations are specific to diabetes or hold across conditions. Life expectancy is included because it comes from death records rather than the PLACES model, so a pattern that appears there cannot be explained by how PLACES builds its estimates. (Higher life expectancy is better, so signs are reversed.)

In [48]:
COMPARE = ["diabetes_pct", "copd_pct", "obesity_pct", "life_expectancy"]
rows = {}
for outcome in COMPARE:
    sub = analysis.dropna(subset=[outcome])
    rows[LABELS[outcome]] = {"n": len(sub),
        **{LABELS[p]: partial_corr(sub, outcome, p, CONTROLS) for p in PREDICTORS}}
outcome_table = pd.DataFrame(rows).T
display(outcome_table.style.format("{:.2f}").format("{:,.0f}", subset=["n"]))

short = {"Diabetes (%)": "Diabetes", "COPD (%)": "COPD", "Obesity (%)": "Obesity",
         "Life expectancy (yrs)": "Life expectancy"}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 3.8))
sns.heatmap(outcome_table.drop(columns="n").T.rename(columns=short), annot=True, fmt=".2f",
            cmap=DIVERGING, vmin=-0.6, vmax=0.6, linewidths=2, linecolor="white",
            cbar_kws={"label": "Partial correlation"}, ax=ax)
ax.set(title="Associations after adjusting for log income and % rural, by outcome",
       xlabel="Outcome  (note: higher life expectancy is better)", ylabel="")
ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=0)
ax.grid(False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
  n Some college (%) Uninsured adults (%) log(1 + PCPs per 100k) Unemployment (%)
Diabetes (%) 2,799 -0.45 0.36 -0.14 0.18
COPD (%) 2,799 -0.48 -0.02 -0.04 0.14
Obesity (%) 2,799 -0.20 -0.07 -0.09 -0.04
Life expectancy (yrs) 2,727 0.32 -0.19 0.15 -0.07

What it shows:

  • Education is the most consistent finding: it keeps a substantial association with diabetes (−0.45), COPD (−0.48) and, importantly, life expectancy (+0.32). Because life expectancy is computed independently of PLACES, the education result is unlikely to be an artifact of PLACES using education in its model.
  • Uninsurance matters for diabetes (+0.36) and life expectancy (−0.19) but not for COPD or obesity (both near 0). Its link may be specific to conditions where diagnosis and ongoing care matter.
  • Obesity barely responds to any predictor once income and rurality are controlled (all |r| ≤ 0.20).

4. Planned Models¶

The EDA points to two models, one for each part of our question.

Model 1: Hypothesis test — does anything matter beyond income?¶
Dependent variable diabetes_pct (age-adjusted diagnosed diabetes, %)
Control variables log_income, rural_pct
Independent variables of interest some_college_pct, uninsured_adults_pct, log_pcp, unemployment_pct
Method Multiple linear regression (OLS, statsmodels) with standard errors clustered by state (EDA 9)
Hypotheses For each predictor, H₀: β = 0 vs. H₁: β ≠ 0, two-sided, α = 0.05 with a Bonferroni correction for four tests. A joint F-test compares the full model with the controls-only model (H₀: all four βs = 0)
Evidence from EDA Partial correlations of −0.45 (education) and +0.36 (uninsurance) and an R² gain of 0.13 suggest at least two predictors will remain significant. All VIFs are below 2
Robustness checks Repeat with COPD, obesity and life expectancy as outcomes; add state fixed effects; add the share of non-Hispanic Black residents (race is part of the PLACES model and the state pattern in EDA 9 is concentrated in the Deep South)

Model 2: Prediction — do these conditions improve accuracy in new places?¶
Target diabetes_pct
Feature sets Baseline: log_income, rural_pct. Full: baseline + the four predictors + child_poverty_pct (overlap between features hurts interpretation, not prediction)
Algorithms Linear regression and a random forest regressor (scikit-learn). The forest can capture curved effects and interactions without us specifying them
Validation GroupKFold cross-validation with states as groups: every test fold contains only states the model never saw in training, so it cannot score well just by learning state averages (EDA 9)
Metrics Root mean squared error (percentage points) and R² on held-out states, comparing full vs. baseline
Interpretation Permutation importance on held-out folds to see which features the model relies on

If the full model clearly reduces error on unseen states, community conditions add predictive value beyond income. If it barely helps, that supports the "it's mostly a poverty problem" interpretation.

5. Findings So Far and Limitations¶

Key findings so far¶

  1. Diabetes prevalence varies nearly fourfold across counties and falls sharply with income, especially among the poorest counties (EDA 2, 3, 6).
  2. Rural counties' higher diabetes rates are mostly explained by their lower incomes (EDA 4).
  3. After controlling for income and rurality, education and insurance coverage still show substantial associations with diabetes. Physician supply and unemployment show weak ones (EDA 7–9).
  4. The education association also appears in life expectancy, which does not depend on PLACES' modeling (EDA 10).

Limitations¶

  • Associations, not causes. These are observational county-level data. Results describe counties, not the individuals living in them.
  • Model-based outcomes. PLACES estimates are built partly from education and poverty (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2025a, 2025c). The life expectancy check reduces this concern but cannot remove it entirely.
  • Diagnosed diabetes only. Places with poor access to care may under-diagnose, understating prevalence where access is worst.
  • Missing states and small counties. Kentucky and Pennsylvania are excluded, and 157 small counties lack physician data.
  • Different reference years. PLACES uses 2023 survey data while CHR measures come from several source years.
  • Equal weighting. Every county counts equally regardless of population.
